newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy's Prodi runs into trouble over tax, pensions.
newsitem.headline: Italy's Prodi runs into trouble over tax, pensions.

text.p: Italy's centre-left government, pushing ahead with its drive to prepare for European monetary union, faced double trouble on Thursday over a controversial "Euro-tax" and the explosive issue of pensions reform.
Divisions in Prime Minister Romano Prodi's six-month-old coalition over the tax came as a blow in the week he triumphantly took the lira back into Europe's Exchange Rate Mechanism (ERM).

"With the ink on the signature of the lira's return to the ERM still wet and part of the budget still to be defined, it would be a tragedy if the prospect of political instability were to appear unexpectedly," La Stampa newspaper said in an editorial.

Next year's unpopular Euro-tax, designed to help Italy become a founder member of a single European currency in 1999, exposed splits within the government on Wednesday when Foreign Minister Lamberto Dini rejected the government's plans.

Prodi also angered trades union leaders with tentative steps to start reviewing a key pension reform deal a year earlier than scheduled in order to complete it before European Union states are judged on their fitness for monetary union in early 1998.
"A general strike is not a sport," Pietro Larizza, leader of the UIL union confederation, said. "But if the government touches pensions, it forces us into it."
Sergio D'Antoni, leader of the CISL confederation, promised Prodi a million people on the streets in Rome, as happened in 1994 over pensions in the biggest protest since World War Two.

The 12.5 trillion lire ($8.3 billion) Euro-tax is a key piece of Prodi's tough 1997 budget, which aims to prune 62.5 trillion lire off next year's deficit and spur Italy's hopes of joining economic and monetary union (EMU) from the start.

In a further slap for the government, the influential former chairman of car company Fiat, Gianni Agnelli and his successor Cesare Romiti, said it would not be a "tragedy" if Italy lagged a little. Ministers responded with sharp criticism.
The government bowed to widespread pressure to revise its Euro-tax plans and announced changes late on Wednesday.
Dini, who leads the small centrist Italian Renewal party in Prodi's coalition, dismissed the proposed alterations as "completely insufficient."
The party has worked out an alternative set of measures it says would spread the tax burden more fairly and has submitted these as an amendment for debate in the Senate (upper house).
Massimo D'Alema, whose Democratic Party of the Left is the biggest in government, criticised Dini, telling a party meeting his move unacceptably altered the balance of the Euro-tax.
The budget -- minus the Euro-tax element -- was passed with help from the hardline Communist Refoundation party in the lower Chamber of Deputies, where opposition parties staged a boycott.
Communist Refoundation, whose support will be crucial to secure final approval of the Euro-tax, warned on Wednesday that "storm clouds" were gathering.
Sergio Cofferati, leader of Italy's biggest union confederation CGIL, said he did not object in principle to the government's Euro-tax changes provided the poor were protected.

But he accused the government of trying to provoke a general strike after Prodi asked a body monitoring pension spending to study the impact of possible changes to the rules, introduced in 1995 and technically not due for review until 1998.
Economic commentators say Italy needs to restructure its pension spending to help cut the state deficit and meet the strict criteria for single currency membership.
